Earnings are highly cyclical and volatile, with net income falling 57% year-over-year [D01].

final.memo:
Lehman Brothers is a global financial services firm involved in fixed-income intermediation, equity execution, and investment banking [D01]. We find it difficult to evaluate the business because it relies on complex, volatile trading activities and the confidence of creditors who can shorten their investment horizons at any time [D05].

Unlike the wonderful businesses we prefer, this firm lacks a durable competitive advantage and sufficient pricing power to maintain stability during market stress [D06]. We saw this clearly in the recent quarter, where fixed-income revenue plummeted 88% and overall net income fell 57% [D01].

The business requires a massive capital base that is prone to significant write-downs, as evidenced by the $1.8 billion in negative mark-to-market adjustments reported recently [D01], [D05]. With ROE dropping to 8.6% from 24.4% in the prior year, the returns on capital are simply not the consistent, high-quality results we seek [D01].

While some may see the stock trading near its $39.45 book value as a bargain, we believe this price fails to account for the fundamental fragility of the business [D01], [D02]. Investing in a firm that is one liquidity shock away from insolvency is not a game we play; we would rather hold cash than risk permanent loss of capital [D05], [D08].

We prefer to allocate our capital to businesses like American Express or Wells Fargo, where we have high confidence in the durability of their moats [D08]. Lehman Brothers is a high-risk gamble on market conditions rather than an investment in a wonderful business at a fair price [D05], [D08].
